realLife:
THE MOMENT (my own working, approximate): at 8:35 EDT on Oct 16 2026 on Lady's Island the sun is about 12-13 deg up in the east-southeast (azimuth ~110 deg). That is 1h08 after the 7:27 sunrise and about half an hour past the end of golden hour (+6 deg comes at about 8:05). So the light is a pale butter-gold, warmer than noon but no longer amber or rose. In the scene's terms litC at goldK 0 is about #FFF1CC. The air is 70F at 88% RH over a tidal river after a calm night: a light coastal haze, no fog. Looking into the sun, you see everything in front of it from its shaded side. The picture becomes contre-jour: a darker, cooler tree against the brightest part of the sky, with the light living only at edges and in whatever is thin.

SKY BEHIND THE CROWN: near the sun the sky is not blue. A broad bright aureole (forward scattering by humid haze) runs pale cream to warm white for roughly 10-15 deg around the disc, then grades out to a washed pale blue. The crown is read against this, so it looks darker than it is.

THE SUN IN THE GAPS: where it shows through the crown, the eye does not see a yellow disc. It sees a point too bright to look at, cream-white. Its glare blooms over the leaf edges round it, so the gap looks bigger than it is, and thin twigs and leaves right over it disappear into the light. The eye also sees a faint fine radiating corona. A camera's tidy even-spiked sunstar comes from the aperture blades and is not what the eye sees.

CROWN OUTLINE (light wrap and rim): a crisp bright fringe runs round the canopy's edge. It is widest and brightest on the stretch of outline nearest the sun, thins as it runs round, and is gone where the outline faces away from the sun or lies far from it in the frame. Live oak leaves are small, thick, leathery and glossy above, with pale grey felted undersides. So on this tree the rim is not the neon green glow of a maple. It is a silvery-to-gold fringe: the waxy tops glint and the felted undersides scatter light forward. At the outline nearest the sun the dark edge itself dissolves, because the light eats into the silhouette.

LEAVES NEAR THE SUN: only where a single layer of leaves stands between eye and sun does light come through: the thin outer scallops and the twig ends right beside the disc. There the colour is olive-gold to warm yellow-green, like stained glass. A thick evergreen leaf passes much less light than a thin one, so this is a narrow band inside the rim, not the whole crown. Where two leaves overlap it goes dark again (Leonardo advised painters to leave out that confusing overlap).

LEAVES FACING US: the body of the crown is in its own shade, lit only by the blue sky behind the viewer and a little warm bounce off the water and mud. It is a deep, cool, desaturated blue-green, a good step or two darker than the same leaves at noon, with little texture showing. The depth order inverts. The back of the crown is the side the sun is on, so where it shows through gaps it is lighter and warmer than the front. Backlight makes the far side lighter, the opposite of frontlight.

SPANISH MOSS (the famous part): the strands are covered in grey trichome scales that scatter light. Dry, they make the moss silver-grey. Wet, they go clear and the moss turns green. Moss hanging between the eye and a low sun lights up like spun silver-gold. Where: the loose outer fringe and the trailing tips of every curtain within roughly 10-25 deg of the sun glow brightest, as a halo outlining each beard, and thin wisps light up whole. The dense core of a curtain stays a muted grey-olive, darker than at noon because it is seen from its shaded side. Curtains far from the sun in the frame do not glow at all. A curtain inside the crown that a beam reaches through a gap lights up like a lamp hung in the dark canopy: the single most magical note such a scene has. The colour is pale champagne to silvery cream (the sun's colour on a near-white scatterer), warmer near sunrise. Dew-wet or rain-wet moss is greener and glows less.

TRUNK AND LIMBS: dark, cool, violet-brown-grey silhouettes, bark detail lost in shade. The long sinuous horizontal limbs read as dark calligraphy across the bright gaps. A hairline of warm light appears on a limb's edge only where the limb crosses the glow near the sun.

SHAFTS THROUGH THE MOSS: in this air, faint at most. Sunbeams are volumes of lit haze between shadows, so they need four things: something in the air to scatter (haze, mist, smoke), a low sun, gaps in the crown and moss, and a dark backdrop behind the beam. They fan out from the sun's position. In an 88% RH haze a whisper of pale beams can show against the tree's own shade and the shaded bank, never against the bright sky. The strong glowing shafts through moss in the classic Lowcountry photograph come with river mist or thinning fog.

SHADOW TOWARD THE VIEWER: at ~12.5 deg a shadow is about 4.4x the height of what casts it. The oak's shadow runs straight at the viewer, widening, and off the bottom of the frame. The bank at the oak's foot, its grass and the flat in front lie in cool blue-green shade, dappled with small elliptical pinholes of sun from gaps in the crown. Its edge is sharp near the trunk and softens with distance. On the river it barely registers, because water shows reflection: there is only a duller patch on the turbid water where the sky's sheen is missing. The oak's dark shape reflects in the water by the bank. Outside the shadow, the wet mud and the water toward the sun shine with a bright silver-gold sheen.

WHITE EGRETS AND IBIS IN THE CROWN: white in shade is not white. A bird inside the crown is a pale cool lavender-grey, lit by the blue sky. Birds on the sun-side edge or the top of the crown wear a broad brilliant warm rim on head, neck, back and wing edge, because feathers scatter like fur, so the rim is wider and hotter than a leaf's and nearly flares. Birds deep in the crown get no rim. Bills glow when backlit: the egret's yellow goes amber, and the ibis's coral face and bill a deep lit coral. A perched ibis hides its black wingtips.

AS THE SUN CLIMBS OUT OF THE CROWN:
- Sun behind the dense crown: the crown is darkest, with a glow ring round the outline nearest the sun and the sun only twinkling through gaps. Shafts are most likely now.
- Sun at the crown's thin edge: the brightest, most fiery moment. The rim is at its widest, the glare eats the edge, and the moss beside it blazes.
- Sun a disc or more clear above the crown: the rim pulls back to the top edge, the glare no longer overlaps leaves, translucency stays only in the topmost scallops, and moss glows only on upper curtains near the sun. The shadow shortens.
- Past ~25-30 deg, and swinging south: ordinary side and top light (lit edge toward the sun, crescent away), moss silvery on its sunny side, no glow.
- Earlier, nearer sunrise: the same picture, warmer (rose to amber), dimmer, with longer shadows.

WEATHER:
- Thin cloud: the disc is softened, and the rim, translucency and moss glow are narrower and paler. Shadows go soft and weak, and there are no shafts.
- Overcast or a veiled sun: no rim, no glow, no shadow. A flat darker crown stands against bright grey, with plain grey moss.
- Haze: a broader, whiter aureole and lower contrast, with the silhouette lifted slightly. The far shore toward the sun dissolves into warm pale haze, and faint shafts can show.
- Fog: depth is graded, with the near limbs darkest and the back crown pale, and the sun a white disc or gone. Thinning fog with the sun breaking through gives the full spectacle of beams through the moss, with the beams the star and the moss glow softer. Dense fog: none of it.

parts.look: Pale warm cream-white around the sun (about #FFF6DC at the core, #F3E8C6 a little out), grading to washed pale blue over roughly 10-15 deg. This is sky colour, a broad gradient behind everything on the still back layer. It is what makes the crown read dark.
parts.strength: medium, broader and whiter with humidity/haze, gone under overcast

parts.look: A small, flat cream-white point (litC lightened toward white), not a yellow disc. One or two flat stepped halo rings (about 1.6x and 2.4x the disc, at ~.45 and ~.2 opacity of litC) are drawn over the nearest leaf edges so the gap looks bigger and the edges are eaten. A few of the scene's own tapered cream rays (long and short, uneven, 4-7 of them, never an even 6- or 8-spike lens star) poke out only where there is sky.
parts.strength: strong at the point, tiny in area

parts.look: A hard-edged flat band inside the silhouette along the outline that faces the sun's screen position. Cream-gold (litC, about #FFF1CC this morning) at the outer edge. Widest nearest the sun (about 2-2.5 screen px at 390), tapering to zero about 90 deg round the outline and by about half a crown-width away from the sun. Silvery-gold rather than green, because live oak leaves glint and their felted undersides scatter.
parts.strength: strong near the sun, falling to none

parts.look: A second flat band just inside the rim, only on the thin outer scallops and twig ends within about a quarter crown-width of the disc. Olive-gold to warm yellow-green (about #C9C45C, up to #D8D27C right at the sun). Narrow (2-4 px), because the leaves are thick. Overlaps stay dark, with no doubled leaf-shadow mess.

parts.part: Front crown, the leaves facing us
parts.look: The bulk of the canopy goes into its own shade. Roughly 25-35% darker than the day leaf (#71904E toward about #4C6648), shifted toward blue-green and about 20% less saturated, from the blue sky behind the viewer. Little internal detail. Paper grain stays on it so it never becomes a black hole.
parts.strength: strong (the contrast is what makes the glow read)

parts.look: Inverted from frontlight: the back leaves are on the sun's side, so near the sun they read lighter and warmer than the front (#55733F toward about #8E9B55, with the far ones taking a little warm haze). Away from the sun they stay as they are.

parts.part: Spanish moss within ~10-25 deg of the sun
parts.look: A halo outlining each beard: a flat band of pale champagne-silver (about #F4EDD2, near-white #FFF6DE at the closest) along both edges and over the loose trailing tips. Thin wisps nearest the sun are filled whole with the glow. The hairlines nearest the sun are drawn in the glow colour instead of ink. The dense body goes darker and cooler (#88917A toward about #727A68), and the dark locks stay. On front curtains the glow must be inside each curtain's own sway group, so it moves with it.
parts.strength: strong nearest the sun, the brightest thing in the tree after the sun itself

parts.part: Spanish moss away from the sun / back moss / veil
parts.look: No glow. The front curtains are slightly darker than by day. The far moss near the sun goes paler and warmer (#AEB5A4 toward about #CBC8AE), as haze lit from behind. The veil inside the crown is darker, except a curtain struck by a beam through a gap, which lights up whole in the glow colour like a lamp in the dark crown (at most one or two).
parts.strength: subtle, with one or two strong accents

parts.look: The darkest, coolest mass: wood about #4E3E3B (violet-brown-grey), detail about #33282A, with bark texture suppressed in shade. A hairline warm rim (about #EBCB8C, 0.5-1 px) only on limb edges that cross the glow near the sun. The heavy ink on the underside and on the side away from the sun.

Flat, hard-edged, very low-opacity wedges of litC that fan out from the sun's position through real gaps in the crown and moss. Few (2-5), of uneven width, drawn only over dark backgrounds (the crown's shade, the shaded bank, the shadowed water), fading along their length in 2-3 steps or a linear gradient on a still layer. Never over the bright sky. They never move.
parts.strength: this morning a whisper (opacity ~.06-.10) or none, up to ~.25 in thinning mist or fog with the sun out

parts.look: One flat, cool, semi-transparent shape from the trunk's foot toward the bottom of the frame, widening as it comes, about 4.4x the tree's height at 12.5 deg, so it runs off the frame. Blue-green on grass, cool violet-brown on mud. A few small elliptical sun-fleck holes where the crown has gaps. Its edge stepped (a crisp umbra near the trunk, a paler penumbra band further out), never blurred.
parts.strength: medium on land (~.4 opacity), weak on water (~.12-.15)

parts.part: Wet mud and water toward the sun (outside the oak's shadow)
parts.look: Contre-jour sheen: the wet edge and the wet mud and water facing the sun go bright silver-gold. Inside the oak's shadow there is no sheen. The oak's dark reflection sits in the water by the bank.
parts.strength: medium, gated by the same backlight

parts.look: Two flat tones. The shade body is pale cool lavender-grey (about #C8CDD8), never pure white. A broad hard rim of warm cream-white (about #FFF4D6) on head, neck, back and wing edge facing the sun, only for birds near the sun or on the crown's top or sun-side edge. Birds deep in the crown have no rim. The yellow bill reads as glowing amber when rimmed.
parts.strength: rim strong when near the sun, otherwise just the cool shade tone

parts.look: The same two tones as the egret. The coral bare face and decurved bill go deep glowing coral (about #E2765A) when rimmed and a darker coral-brown in shade. The black wingtips are hidden when perched.

parts.part: Far line, bridge and steeples toward the sun
parts.look: Aerial perspective goes warm and bright toward the sun rather than blue. The far wood nearest the sun dissolves toward the aureole's cream with low contrast, and the bridge's truss reads as a pale, lifted silhouette.

parts.part: Spartina tips on the near bank
parts.look: Only where the grass stands near the sun line in the frame: a thin gold glint on the blade tips. Away from the sun, nothing. The grass on the oak's shaded bank stays cool and unlit.

storybook:
A storybook painter does backlight with value, colour temperature and edges. It is never a photographic effect. The rule of thumb: the tree becomes one darker, cooler shape against the lightest sky in the picture, and the light is a thin, hard-edged gift along the edges nearest the sun. Keep every shape and every part exactly as drawn. Backlight is a different colour plan on the same parts, and it is restrained: if the whole crown glows, nothing does.

1. Value plan: group the crown, the wood and the moss bodies into a shadow family, darker, cooler and less saturated than by day (the sky behind the viewer fills them blue), with paper grain kept over it. Invert the depth order near the sun: the back leaves and the far moss, on the sun's side, are lighter and warmer than the front. Eyvind Earle's lesson, as Pete Docter put it, applies: the light decides where the detail goes, so the bark and leaf texture in the shade drop out and only the lit edges carry detail.

2. Three flat tones for backlit foliage, like Prince of Persia's few discrete shades:
- the cool shadow body;
- a narrow warm through-light band (olive-gold);
- a cream-gold rim at the very edge.
Each is a flat shape cut from the silhouette itself, the way the kit already makes the lit edge (the silhouette masked by an offset copy). The offset points toward the sun's screen position and its width scales with how close that part is to the sun. It is effectively the kit's lit edge, made 2-3x wider nearest the sun and fading to nothing a half crown-width away. That way it adds nothing to the footprint, and it works with the existing veil, litK and goldK so thin cloud, fog and golden hour fall out for free.

3. Lost and found edges, the inked part. Along the stretch of outline nearest the sun, the ink line is lost: it thins to nothing or takes the rim colour (a coloured line, the trick cel painters use for light). Thin twigs and moss hairlines right over the sun are drawn in light or dropped, because the light eats them. The heavier ink moves to where the shadow side now is: the undersides of the scallops and limbs and the side away from the sun. That keeps the house rule (ink heavier on the shadow side) true in backlight.

4. Glow as shape, never blur. Around a sun peeking through a gap, use one or two concentric flat halo rings of litC at falling opacity (a posterized bloom), laid over the leaf edges nearest the disc so they look eaten. Add the scene's own tapered cream rays from the header and icon, long and short and uneven, only into sky. That carries the sunstar in the house drawing and not a lens's. The sky's aureole can be a broad gradient, because it is sky colour on the still back layer. Glow on objects is always a hard flat band.

5. Moss is the star. Draw the backlit moss as a flat silver-champagne halo band along both edges of each curtain and over its loose tips, with the thinnest wisps filled whole, the hair strokes near the sun in the light colour, and the body darker. On the front curtains this lives inside each curtain's own sway group on #sceneMoss (the existing sheen part is the natural home, used on both edges instead of one side), so it rides the sway and adds no animation. Paint one or two curtains in the crown's shade fully lit by a beam through a gap.

6. Shafts are few flat translucent wedges with crisp sides. They fan out from the sun, cross only darks, fade in steps and never move. They sit on a still layer above the crown (#sceneNear), and this morning they are almost invisible.

7. The cast shadow is one flat cool shape coming at the viewer, with a stepped penumbra and a handful of elliptical sun-fleck holes, laid on the still bank and mud and much weaker on the water.

8. White birds take two flat tones: a cool lavender shade body and a hard warm rim on the sun side, the rim broader than a leaf's because feathers scatter like fur.

9. Warm light, cool shade: the only warm notes in the tree are the rim, the through-light and the moss halo, plus a whisper of warm bounce from the bright water on the undersides of the lowest limbs.

References for the attitude: Earle's flat shapes where light places the detail. Kazuo Oga at Ghibli, who paints from observation but keeps only the essential point. Jonathan Green, Beaufort County's own Lowcountry painter of flat colour fields. Prince of Persia 2008's cel-shaded, watercolour-like few discrete shades.

Everything new and still goes on the still layers (#sceneSvg, #sceneNear). Only the front moss's glow lives on #sceneMoss, inside the groups that already sway. No SVG filter anywhere, no new animation, and every draw stays seeded.
avoid: Any photographic lens flare: hexagonal or round ghosts, rainbow rings, streaks across the frame, chromatic fringes
A camera sunstar with an even 6/8/12/18-spike pattern, or a starburst big enough to cover the crown; use the scene's own uneven tapered rays, small
Gaussian-blur glow, bloom or an outer-glow halo on objects, and any SVG filter on anything inside a moving layer; glow on objects is a hard flat band
Glowing the whole crown or tinting it yellow; the glow is confined to the edges and to parts near the sun, and the rest of the tree goes darker so the glow reads
Neon green translucency across the canopy; live oak leaves are thick and leathery, so through-light is a narrow olive-gold band on the thin outer scallops next to the sun only
Lighting the leaves that face us, or putting a lit edge on the side away from the sun; in backlight the front face is the shadow side
Keeping the day's depth order near the sun (back leaves darker than the front); in backlight the sun-side back of the crown is lighter and warmer
A heavy dark ink line along the outline nearest the sun; lose it or colour it there, and move the weight to the undersides and the side away from the sun
Moss drawn as a yellow or white fill, or glowing everywhere; it is a silver-champagne halo on the edges and tips, with whole thin wisps lit, only within ~10-25 deg of the sun
Pure white egrets and ibis inside the shaded crown (they read as holes); white in shade is cool lavender-grey, and only near-sun birds get a warm rim
Amber or rose light at 8:35; golden hour ended about 8:05, so the light is pale butter-gold (litC with goldK at 0)
God rays in clear dry air, rays drawn over the bright sky, rays that do not fan out from the sun's position, or rays that move or pulse
A cast shadow falling away from the viewer or to the wrong side, a shadow as dark on water as on land, or a blurred shadow edge instead of a stepped penumbra
Bark texture or leaf detail in the shaded front; detail goes where the light is
A pitch-black silhouette; humid air and sky fill keep the shade a deep cool blue-green with paper grain
Sparkle confetti, dew glitter animations or any new animation; the only motion is the existing moss sway carrying its own glow
Adding leaves, moss or birds to make the effect; same drawing, new colour plan
Letting any of it touch Porters Neck's marsh scene or Shady Spring's ridge
